summary:
Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted at the border provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded on entry. This guidance is set out in the official WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 safety and travel information.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited under Dutch law. Gender expression has been an explicitly protected ground under the Dutch Equal Treatment Act since March 2019, and since February 2023 sexual orientation and disability are written into Article 1 of the Constitution. From 1 July 2025 a discriminatory motive is codified in the Criminal Code as a ground for increasing penalties, following a private-member's bill by Timmermans and Bikker, alongside expanded rights for victims and protection of victim data.

Official victimisation figures are high. More than 10% of LGBTIQ+ people in the Netherlands have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people. The 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence; in 2022, one third of police reports concerning discrimination related to sexual orientation.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is climbing. Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, according to figures relayed by Transgender Netwerk. Reports concerning transgender people rose 51% in a single year, from 264 to 399. The LGBTI organisation COC described the trend as extremely worrying and noted that only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were secured last year.

During the opening of WorldPride Amsterdam in 2026, more than 70 people reported discrimination through the RITA platform, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and participants in the Pride Walk; RITA warned that these reports represent only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened its 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during the event to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. Mayor Halsema told the council that the city would tackle discrimination and violent incidents as a priority during World Pride, with police, enforcers and organisers agreeing to act quickly. Recent Prides drew between 25 and 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

Same-sex marriage is legal, non-binary people are legally recognised, and conversion therapy is banned, with the prohibiting bill ratified on 8 September 2026. Access to gender-affirming care is established: the 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, top surgery is available to patients over 16, and in July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing the harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Bathroom access is protected.

Detention carries specific risks. No law, regulation or official policy currently governs the placement of transgender detainees in the Netherlands; the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) places people according to the gender designation in municipal population records together with case-by-case factors. Transgender detainees are frequently held on an 'Extra Care Facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Courts have treated placement on a wing not matching a detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier.
tangentialFactors:
The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026, and a comparative rights dataset places it second of 121 regions as a good place for LGBTI people, with 22% high public support figures for LGBT openness. These aggregate rankings sit alongside the rising incident counts recorded by police, so a high international score should not be read as an absence of street-level hostility.

Attitudes among young people are moving in the opposite direction to the legal framework. A Utrecht University and Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys falling from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025. A 2018 Statistics Netherlands survey found 11.4% of LGBTQ youth faced online bullying and harassment, more than double the rate for heterosexual young people, and a 2020 Movisie estimate put homeless LGBTQ youth at 900 to 2,000, three times the heterosexual rate, with rejection at home a stated cause.

Police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P), but Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime', according to the OSCE/ODIHR national framework page. The gap between recording practice and statutory definition helps explain the distance between 4,800 reports and six convictions in a year.

Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality was declassified as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. The age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1971, ending the 1911 Article 248bis rule that had set 21 for same-sex activity.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a letter from a medical expert, falling short of self-determination, and the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months. The Transgender Act, which would have introduced self-identification, was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation has been offered to people sterilised under earlier rules; legal gender recognition became administrative under a December 2013 law that took effect in 2014, removing the surgery and sterilisation requirement imposed by the 1984-85 laws.

Employment and housing discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. The government-financed religious-school 'single fact construction' loophole that allowed staff to be fired, as in a 2005 case concerning a teacher in a same-sex relationship, was closed by bills passed in 2014 and 2015, effective 1 July 2015, so LGBTQ students and teachers cannot be dismissed on those grounds.

Dutch insurance fully covers PrEP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices, projected to save €33 million in HIV treatment costs. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012.

Placement practice for transgender detainees rests on unpublished guidance rather than statute. DJI confirmed to the Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights that placement is based on the gender designation in the BRP municipal records alongside case-by-case factors including gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background and physical or mental health, while DIZ was drafting guidelines that remain unpublished. NJCM documented a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing on arrival before transfer to an Extra Care Facility wing; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; and sentencing rulings by the Limburg court of 17 October 2017 (ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and the The Hague appeals court of 29 June 2020 (ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108), the latter concerning a trans man in a women's prison. NJCM asked the Minister for Legal Protection, Weerwind, in a letter of 21 February 2024 to create rules aligned with CPT standards placing transgender detainees by gender identity, noting that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two source characterisations of hate-crime protection do not align and the inventory does not resolve them. The government's own 1 July 2025 announcement describes a discriminatory motive written into the Criminal Code as a ground for increasing penalties, while the Equaldex dataset states that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. Whether gender identity is expressly named as an aggravating ground, or reaches it indirectly through existing protected categories, is not settled by the sources held here.

The OSCE/ODIHR page records that Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime', which bears on how the police-recorded figures should be read, but the sources do not state whether a statutory definition is pending.

Whether the NJCM advice of February 2024 produced rules aligning transgender detainee placement with CPT standards is not sourced. The letter documents that DIZ was drafting unpublished guidelines at that date; no later status is available in this inventory.

The RITA figure of more than 70 discrimination reports during the opening of WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 is explicitly described by the platform as a fraction of the total, so no reliable count of incidents during the event exists in these sources. The 25 to 45 reports cited for recent Prides are baseline figures rather than a 2026 total.

Victimisation percentages from the government page are national LGBTIQ+ figures with a transgender subset of 17%; the inventory does not date the underlying survey or state whether it covers visitors or residents.
